Five humans · one suspiciously large backlog

We build with AI.
We still read the diff.

We’re five computer science students exploring what happens when human ideas meet machine-speed code. We like clever tools, thoughtful design, and knowing why the tests are red before asking a chatbot to “fix everything.”

Team strategy: automate the boring bits. Keep the humans for the weird bits.

The people behind the pull requests

Meet the team

Five perspectives. Zero tolerance for mysterious bugs.

Mohammad

M.Sc. Computer Science · 1st semester

Into full-stack development and gaming, Mohammad will happily spend 40 hours with a story-driven game—but a 30-second test build tests his sanity. He sees AI as an eager junior developer: brilliant at boilerplate, prone to subtle logic bugs, and deserving of a thorough review.

Fun fact: 40-hour games get zero skips; 30-second builds get side-eye.

🔥 AI doesn’t make bad developers good; it just helps them generate catastrophic technical debt at record speed.

Nithya

M.Sc. Computer Science · 7th semester, thesis stage

Nithya is interested in distributed systems and cloud architecture, plus badminton and board games. She values AI for familiar tasks, but complex legacy code and concurrency are where confident guesses can become very expensive. Her copilot still needs an experienced pilot.

Fun fact: Her thesis abstract has had more rewrites than her code has recompiles.

🔥 AI autocomplete hasn’t eliminated bugs; it has just made them compile much faster.

Rafee

M.Sc. Computer Science · 1st semester

A frontend UI/UX enthusiast and React/Next.js explorer, Rafee also enjoys table tennis and photography. He judges coffee shops by Wi-Fi stability and latency to GitHub. AI can be a brilliant interactive tutor—as long as the student learns the concept, not just the copy-paste shortcut.

Fun fact: Coffee shops are judged by their Wi-Fi latency to GitHub.

🔥 If you can’t debug code without an LLM, you are the copilot, not the agent.

Raghvendra

M.Sc. Computer Science · 3rd semester

Raghvendra focuses on machine-learning infrastructure and data engineering, with hiking and chess for balance. AI helps him prototype and clear boilerplate, but missing context and deprecated methods make it a poor substitute for architectural judgment.

Fun fact: Four hours automating five minutes of work? An investment.

🔥 90% of current “AI agent” workflows are just fragile while loops wrapped around regex parsers.

Sayemah

M.Sc. Computer Science · 1st semester

Sayemah brings together calligraphy, cooking, travel, and human-computer interaction. She sees AI as a fast path to creative prototypes, but great software needs communication, empathy, and aesthetic intention—not only syntactically valid code.

Fun fact: A complex recipe succeeds first try; one curly brace can ruin the evening.

🔥 Prompt engineering is not the future of software engineering; thoughtful human design is.

Our shared outlook

The Future of Software Engineering

We don’t think engineers are going away. We think the job is moving up a level: less typing boilerplate, more deciding what should exist—and proving it works when reality gets weird.

  • AI as a capable assistant. It can speed up prototypes, explanations, and repetitive work, but its output still needs context and review.
  • Humans set direction. Engineers will define requirements, architecture, privacy boundaries, accessibility, and the failure cases an agent might miss.
  • Verification matters more. Testing, reliability, security, and checking the diff remain essential—even when the diff arrives at machine speed.
  • Design stays human. Empathy, collaboration, and choosing the right problem are not syntax errors that autocomplete can fix.
